# Cosmic Sources {#sources-section}

## Where jets get their power {#cosmic-messengers}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Tidal disruption

<video class="slide-video media-height-lg" style="--media-max-height: 620px;" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" poster="media/jets/jet_launch_en.jpg" src="media/jets/jet_launch_en.mp4" aria-label="From a star to a jet: tidal disruption, returning debris and a schematic magnetic engine."></video>

::: {.media-caption}
Computed debris orbits, schematic magnetic engine.
:::

### AGN

- Gas feeds an accretion disc around a supermassive black hole.
- Magnetic fields can extract rotational energy and carry it into a jet.
- The gas supply can sustain activity beyond a single stellar disruption.
- **Blazars:** the jet points close to our line of sight.

::: {.media-caption}
[Blandford, Meier & Readhead, Relativistic Jets in AGN](https://arxiv.org/abs/1812.06025)
:::

### Gamma-ray bursts

| Scenario | Fuel for the central engine |
| --- | --- |
| Massive-star collapse | Stellar material falls onto the compact remnant. |
| Compact-object merger | Debris forms a temporary accretion disc. |

- Accretion onto a black hole or the spin of a strongly magnetized neutron star can power a relativistic outflow.
- The engine operates during a transient event.

::: {.media-caption}
[P. Mészáros, Gamma-Ray Bursts](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0605208)
:::

### Cosmic messengers

- Charged cosmic rays bend in magnetic fields.
- Photons can scatter or be absorbed.
- Neutrinos can escape dense environments and preserve directional information.

:::

## How jets produce neutrinos {#acceleration-and-confinement}

::: {.panel-tabset}

### Star in the jet

<video class="slide-video media-height-lg" style="--media-max-height: 620px;" controls muted playsinline preload="metadata" poster="media/jets/jet_star_en.jpg" src="media/jets/jet_star_en.mp4" aria-label="A star in an existing jet: a gas shock and stripped cloud, schematic proton acceleration and neutrino production."></video>

::: {.media-caption}
Scenario and calculation: [Barkov, Aharonian & Bosch-Ramon (2010)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1005.5252) · The film illustrates the idea: simplified gas model, schematic protons and neutrinos
:::

### Gas

Accelerated protons collide with nuclei in dense gas.

$$
pp\longrightarrow\pi^{\pm},\,\pi^0+X
$$

**Possible targets:** a stripped stellar envelope or a gas cloud in the jet.

The gas density and the proton residence time control the interaction yield.

::: {.media-caption}
[Wang et al., jet–cloud/star scenario](https://arxiv.org/abs/1809.00601)
:::

### Photons

Accelerated protons interact with a radiation field.

$$
p\gamma\longrightarrow\pi^{\pm},\,\pi^0+X
$$

**Possible targets:** synchrotron photons in the jet, or photons from the
accretion disc and its surroundings.

The pion-production threshold depends on photon energy and collision angle.

::: {.media-caption}
[Murase & Stecker, High-Energy Neutrinos from AGN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03381)
:::

### Confinement

The jet supplies energy. The star creates a shock and a dense target.

$$
r_L=\frac{p}{ZeB}\lesssim R
$$

- A source must retain particles long enough to accelerate them.
- Energy losses and the available time also limit the maximum energy.

### Converter

![](media/theory/converter-cycle.svg){.slide-media .nostretch style="--media-width: 1400px; --media-max-height: 525px;" fig-alt="Schematic of one converter acceleration cycle: a proton in a relativistic jet becomes a neutron, leaves the jet without feeling the magnetic field, becomes a proton again outside and is turned back into the jet by the field, gaining energy of order Gamma squared. Each conversion also emits a neutrino. Paths are illustrative."}

::: {.media-caption}
Charge changes let particles cross the field · Gain $\sim\Gamma^2$ per cycle · [Derishev et al. (2003)](https://arxiv.org/abs/astro-ph/0301263)
:::

:::

## Three messengers, one energy budget {#energy-budget}

**Gamma rays, neutrinos and the most energetic cosmic rays carry similar power.**

![](media/theory/energy-budget.svg){.slide-media .nostretch style="--media-max-height: 560px;" fig-alt="Energy flux E squared times flux versus particle energy from 0.1 GeV to 200 EeV. Fermi-LAT isotropic gamma-ray background points from 0.1 to 820 GeV, the IceCube astrophysical neutrino spectrum per flavour from about 14 TeV to 5 PeV with its 68 percent band, and Pierre Auger cosmic-ray points above 3 EeV. A dashed band shows the Waxman-Bahcall bound per flavour, 0.45 to 2.25 times 1e-8; the neutrino flux reaches it near 100 TeV."}

::: {.media-caption}
Neutrinos per flavour · [Fermi-LAT (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1410.3696) · [IceCube (2026)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.22233v3), band digitized from Fig. 3 · [Auger (2020)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.06486) · Bound: [Waxman & Bahcall (1999)](https://arxiv.org/abs/hep-ph/9807282)
:::

## Production environments {#source-populations}

| Environment | Target for energetic hadrons | Observational test |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Galactic disk | Interstellar gas | Spatially extended emission |
| AGN jet | Gas or radiation | Direction and variability |
| AGN corona (hidden core) | Gas and X-ray photons | Neutrinos brighter than GeV–TeV gamma rays |
| Star-forming environment | Dense gas | Population and diffuse-flux constraints |
| GRB or tidal disruption | Gas or radiation | Time-dependent searches |

**Many faint sources:** the brightest neutrino sources seen so far supply only a
small part of the diffuse flux, so most of it should come from many faint emitters.

::: {.media-caption}
[Murase & Stecker](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03381) · Coronae: [Kheirandish, Murase & Kimura (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.04475) · Populations: [Groth & Ahlers (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.07718)
:::
